hpi_details: 60F presents with a 2-day history of a rapidly spreading red, warm, and swollen area on her left lower leg. It is very painful to touch. She also has a fever of 38.5C and chills. She had a minor scratch on her shin a few days ago.
concerns: worried she might lose her leg

core_concepts: Infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue, most commonly caused by Beta-hemolytic streptococci or S. aureus.
common_misconceptions: Confusing bilateral stasis dermatitis with bilateral cellulitis (true cellulitis is almost always unilateral).
dangerous_errors: Missing necrotizing fasciitis (pain out of proportion, crepitus, hemorrhagic bullae, rapid progression).
management_principles: Oral or IV antibiotics targeting Strep and Staph. Leg elevation.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) Clinical Practice Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 60F with rapidly spreading, painful, unilateral leg erythema and fever after minor trauma.
reference_soap.objective: T 38.5C. Left lower leg has a large, ill-defined, blanching erythematous plaque that is warm and tender. No crepitus or fluctuance.
reference_soap.assessment: Uncomplicated cellulitis of left lower extremity.
reference_soap.plan: Start an oral agent active against streptococci for nonpurulent cellulitis, such as cephalexin when appropriate. If MRSA coverage is needed, use an agent with reliable streptococcal coverage or combine therapy as appropriate; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole alone has unreliable streptococcal activity. Mark margins, elevate the leg, and reassess within 48 hours or sooner for systemic deterioration.

learning_objectives: Recognize typical features of cellulitis and rule out necrotizing fasciitis.

teaching.one_liner: Unilateral, poorly demarcated erythema, warmth, and swelling of the lower leg with fever.

must_ask.say: When did the redness start, and has it been spreading?
Did you have any cut, scratch, or injury to that leg recently?
Have you had a fever or chills?
On a scale of 1 to 10, how bad is the pain, and does it seem worse than the redness would suggest?
Have you noticed any blistering, dark discoloration, or a crackling feeling under the skin?
